Neonates of the Short-tailed pygmy monitor emerge from parchment-shelled eggs weighing approximately 1.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.5 grams], a value that aligns closely with the lower range of hatchling masses documented among diminutive varanid species. Field surveys report the wet weight at birth typically falls between 1 and 2 grams, reflecting the relatively low maternal investment per offspring in this early post-hatching stage. The leathery-shelled eggs are deposited in termite mounds or beneath loose bark, where they incubate under relatively stable thermal regimes. Once the shell-pipping event occurs, the hatchling uses its egg caruncle to rupture the chorion and emerges as a fully independent, precocial juvenile. This modest initial mass places Varanus brevicauda among the smallest of all extant monitor lizards at the moment of emergence, a life-history trait that likely constrains the juvenile’s early foraging options and vulnerability to desiccation in the arid environments it frequents.

Reproductively active adults in this species exhibit a surprisingly low reproductive output for a lizard of their size. Females typically deposit a single clutch each year [F_R_i = a single clutch each year], of two to five eggs each year [Ri = of two to five eggs each year], and available long-term field records indicate that a gravid individual produces, on average, one to two viable offspring per clutch [N_R_i = one to two viable offspring per clutch]. When these two components are combined, the maximum daily reproductive rate under optimal captive conditions at a stable temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] is equivalent to roughly 5 eggs every 365 days [Ri = roughly 5 eggs every 365 days], a pace that underscores the species’ slow life-history strategy relative to other small-bodied varanids that inhabit similar tropical savanna habitats.

Long-term mark-recapture studies performed under controlled thermal conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] have demonstrated that the age at birth from egg deposition to hatching spans approximately 122 days [ab = approximately 122 days], a developmental duration that aligns closely with the 3- to 5-month incubation window reported for other varanids of equivalent egg size. Hatchlings emerge with a fully developed yolk sac that provides endotrophic nutrition during the first several days post-eclosion, after which they must independently capture small invertebrate prey to sustain growth. The relatively protracted 122-day embryonic phase (122 days) [ab = 122 days] is remarkably consistent across studies, likely reflecting the species’ occupation of thermally buffered microhabitats such as deep termitaria, where daily temperature fluctuations are dampened compared to exposed nest sites at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].

Basal metabolic rate measurements obtained from flow-through respirometry trials at 35 °C [T = 35 °C] reveal a maximum resting oxygen consumption of 0.0451 milliliters of oxygen per minute [JOi = 0.0451 milliliters of oxygen per minute], a figure that places Varanus brevicauda among the very lowest mass-specific metabolic rates documented for any varanid lizard. This exceptionally low metabolic demand at 35 °C [T = 35 °C] is thought to be an adaptation to the species’ semi-fossorial habits and its reliance on ephemeral arthropod prey in the arid and semi-arid regions of northwestern Australia. The measured rate is consistent with the general pattern among small-bodied reptiles that inhabit resource-poor environments, where minimizing daily energetic expenditure confers a selective advantage during extended periods of low food availability.

Under captive conditions maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], female Short-tailed pygmy monitors achieve gonadal maturity after a relatively brief pre-reproductive interval of 365 days since hatching [tp = 365 days since hatching], a surprisingly rapid maturation for a reptile that exhibits such extreme longevity. Fully grown adults reach an asymptotic body mass of 17.44 grams [Wwi = 17.44 grams], making this species the smallest varanid in Australia, with an adult weight comparable to that of a large skink rather than its giant congeners. Remarkably, maximum recorded lifespan under controlled laboratory conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] extends to approximately 7,410 days [am = approximately 7,410 days], equating to just over 20 years—an extraordinary longevity for a squamate reptile of this diminutive stature that suggests a markedly slow pace of life compared to similarly sized lizards from other families.
